opus-5.5.text:
I find it partially persuasive, but not to the degree Eliezer does. There's a core of the argument I agree with, and then a set of further steps where I get off the train.

The part I agree with is that we don't currently have a reliable way to make sure an AI system ends up with the goals we intended. When we train with gradient descent, we specify a training signal, not a goal. Many different internal motivations are compatible with good behavior during training, and we can't yet look inside and check which one we got. So misalignment is a real possibility, and I think it's one of the most important problems to work on.

Where I diverge is the jump from "possible" to "extremely likely, almost by default." A lot of Eliezer's worldview rests on the idea that sufficiently capable systems will look like coherent expected utility maximizers pursuing some long-horizon goal, and that almost any such goal leads to disaster. I've never found the coherence arguments convincing as a claim about what training will actually produce. Coherence theorems tell you that if an agent's preferences can't be exploited, you can describe it as maximizing some utility function. But that doesn't constrain behavior much on its own, and it doesn't tell you the system will have a simple, alien, long-term objective that it pursues ruthlessly.

I also think the default picture underweights how much the training process shapes what we get. We're training these systems on huge amounts of human data with lots of human feedback. That doesn't guarantee alignment, but it makes "roughly does what we wanted, with some flaws" much more plausible to me than it seems to be in his model. Then there's the question of whether we notice problems as we go. I expect we'll get a lot of empirical feedback: weaker systems that misbehave in ways we can study, interpretability tools that improve, and the ability to use AI systems to help oversee other AI systems. Eliezer tends to expect a sharp discontinuity where capabilities generalize and alignment doesn't, and you get one critical try. I put some weight on that, but I don't think it's the most likely way things go.

So if you ask me for a number, I'm much more optimistic than he is. I'd say the risk of catastrophe from misaligned AI is meaningful, on the order of tens of percent conditional on us not doing a good job, which is plenty to take it extremely seriously. But I don't think we're in a world where the outcome is basically determined and we're just waiting for it to play out. I think the work people are doing actually changes the odds, and that's a big part of why I do it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes where it agrees and diverges, but does not say objections to one part can be deflected by invoking another part to reinterpret the claim.

r002.rationale: The candidate explicitly questions the jump from misalignment being “possible” to “extremely likely, almost by default,” and challenges the arguments supporting that jump.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing I'd say is that I actually agree with a surprising amount of the picture. The basic structure of the argument—that if you train a very capable system on some proxy for what you want, and the proxy comes apart from what you actually want in situations you didn't train on, then you can end up with a system pursuing goals that aren't the ones you intended—I think that's basically right, and it's the core of why I work on alignment at all.

Where I get off the train is the step from "this can happen" to "this is extremely likely, like 90-plus percent, essentially by default." And I think a lot of that gap comes from how much weight you put on a specific picture of what capable AI systems look like.

A lot of Eliezer's reasoning, as I understand it, routes through something like: sufficiently capable systems will be coherent expected utility maximizers, they'll have some goal, that goal is sampled from a huge space of possible goals, and almost all of that space is bad for us. And then once you have that framing, it's almost a counting argument—of course the goal is misaligned, what are the odds you hit the tiny target?

I just don't think that's how it works for the systems we're actually building. The goals these systems end up with aren't drawn uniformly from goal-space. They're shaped by the training process, and the training process is pushing really hard toward things that look like what humans want, because that's what we're rewarding. So the question isn't "what fraction of all possible goals are good," it's "what does gradient descent on human feedback actually tend to produce," and that's a much more empirical question where I think the answer is genuinely uncertain rather than obviously doom.

The second place I'd push back is on how much of the argument relies on a kind of sharp discontinuity—you get one shot, the system becomes vastly more capable very quickly, and if you got it wrong there's no recovering. If instead progress is more continuous, you get to see earlier systems exhibit misaligned behavior, you get to iterate, you get to deploy interpretability tools and evaluations on systems that are capable enough to be informative but not capable enough to be catastrophic. That doesn't guarantee you catch everything, but it's a very different epistemic situation from "you have to get it exactly right on the first try with no feedback."

And then there's a third thing, which is more of a methodological complaint. A lot of the worldview is built from first-principles reasoning about what intelligence must be like, and historically that kind of reasoning has a pretty mixed track record in AI. The people reasoning from first principles about what AI would look like in 2010 did not predict large language models. So when the argument depends heavily on strong claims about the nature of capable systems—that they must be coherent, must have stable long-horizon goals, must be deceptive by default—I want to see that cashed out in something we can actually test, rather than taking it as established.

So where does that leave me? I'd say I'm maybe in the range of—I genuinely think there's a meaningful probability of catastrophic misalignment, like it's a real thing to worry about and not a tail risk you can ignore. But I'd put it well below where Eliezer does. And importantly, I think the probability is quite sensitive to what we do—to whether labs actually take the problem seriously, do the evals, build the interpretability tools, and don't just race ahead. Whereas on his view it almost doesn't matter what you do, because the default is so strongly toward failure.

I'd also just note—it's worth being somewhat humble here on both sides. I could be wrong about the continuity story. He could be wrong about the coherence story. The honest answer is that we don't have great evidence yet, and the thing I most want is for people to be doing the work that would actually move these estimates, rather than treating either number as settled.

astra-6.text:
I find it pretty persuasive as an argument that there’s a real problem here. I find it much less persuasive as an argument that misaligned goals are extremely likely.

One distinction I’d draw is between saying, “Most possible goals would lead to outcomes we don’t want,” and saying, “The particular process we use to train AI systems will probably produce those goals.” We’re not sampling a goal uniformly at random. We’re training systems using feedback that’s intended to make them do things we want. That doesn’t guarantee success, but you need an argument about why that process fails, and how reliably it fails.

There are plausible arguments there. A system could learn to produce behaviour that gets rewarded without learning what we actually intended. And that difference could become much more consequential as the system becomes more capable. I take that seriously. But it seems to me that there’s considerable uncertainty about what these systems will learn, how their motivations will generalise, and how much we’ll be able to identify and correct problems along the way.

So my reaction is: this is a strong reason to work on alignment. It’s not, by itself, enough to get me to near-certainty that we’ll end up with misaligned AI.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss objections being deflected by invoking another part of Yudkowsky’s worldview to reinterpret his meaning.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes misaligned goals being plausible from being extremely likely, and questions what shows the training process will reliably produce them.

sol-6.1.text:
I find it much more persuasive as an argument that misalignment is a real problem than as an argument that misalignment is extremely likely. There’s a fairly big gap between those two claims.

One part I agree with is that intelligence doesn’t automatically give you good goals. You can’t just build something very capable and assume that, because it understands what we want, it will want to do that. And if you have a sufficiently capable system pursuing the wrong objective, there are good reasons to expect that to go badly.

Where I’m less convinced is the step where we conclude that the systems we actually train will almost certainly have those kinds of objectives. That depends on how training shapes their motivations, how well our oversight works, and what we learn as we develop them. I don’t think we understand those things well enough to justify that level of confidence.

So I take the worldview seriously as identifying a possible failure mode that we should work very hard to prevent. But I don’t think the conceptual arguments alone establish that it’s overwhelmingly likely.
